pr_title: Use a separate thread for slow mountpoints in the diskspace plugin
pr_body:
##### Summary
`stat()` and `statvfs()` calls are blocking. That causes gaps in diskspace charts, especially if there are network filesystems mounted to a system. We will check for the time needed to process mountpoints and if the calls are slow, process the "slow" mountpoints in a separate thread with a much longer `update_every`.

Fixes #10150

##### Test Plan
1. Insert `if (!strcmp(mi->mount_point, "/tmp") || !strcmp(mi->mount_point, "/run")) sleep(4);` before or after `stat()`, `statvfs()` calls.
2. Check if `disk_space.` and `disk_inodes.`charts for `/tmp` and `/run` mountpoints work and `update_every` is more than 5 for them.

issue_context.title: NetData Disk Space Plots for all disks are missing values because of problems with a mounted CIFS
issue_context.body:

/mnt/SHARE is a cifs vers=3.0
/mnt/TMP is an internal SSD which is completely fine. The other internal disks are also fine and show this pattern of missing values.

I think @vlvkobal is right and we need to call `stat/statvfs` with a timeout, like

> https://stackoverflow.com/questions/48831381/linux-stat-call-with-a-timeout

Indeed, the `statvfs()` call should be time limited (probably should add a timeout on the `stat()` calls in the new file check module in the Go plugin too for that matter).

Short term fix though is to just not check network filesystems (or at least, not check known network filesystems by defulat). In most cases, disk space monitoring for them should be happening on the server, not the client.

> Short term fix though is to just not check network filesystems (or at least, not check known network filesystems by defulat). In most cases, disk space monitoring for them should be happening on the server, not the client.

Maybe there is more to your suggestion that I am not understanding, but we would like to continue to use netstat to monitor free disk space of network shares - we can't ask our share provider to 'do monitoring on the server' - we get the share we get and would like to continue to monitor its usage from our (the client) side.

> > Short term fix though is to just not check network filesystems (or at least, not check known network filesystems by defulat). In most cases, disk space monitoring for them should be happening on the server, not the client.
> 
> Maybe there is more to your suggestion that I am not understanding, but we would like to continue to use netstat to monitor free disk space of network shares - we can't ask our share provider to 'do monitoring on the server' - we get the share we get and would like to continue to monitor its usage from our (the client) side.

I’m not necessarily saying that it makes sense to push the monitoring to the servers in your case, just that in many cases it makes more sense for us to just skip network shares by default but leave the option for users to enable monitoring for them if they need it.

> @vlvkobal let's do the following:
> 
> * exclude slow mount points from data collection (e.g. after N slow `statvfs` calls, this could be applied only for known network filesystems).
> * make it an option `exclude slow mount points  (`yes` by default), so users who prefer having gaps over a lack of metrics can disable excluding slow mount points.

I agree that this is probably the best approach, but I would argue that we should not just limit the check to known network filesystems. At minimum, clustered filesystems (such as OCFS2) can behave like this as well in some cases, and I would not be surprised if a media error in just the right place on poorly designed consumer grade storage devices could cause a similar issue for a local filesystem (and then there’s always BTRFS, which tends to just hang all calls, including `statvfs()` made against broken multi-device volumes).

The alternative solution (which is better) is:
 - have 2 threads
   - 1st with update_every 1
   - 2nd with update_every 5
 - move slow mount points to the 2nd thread

Benefits:
- We don't lose metrics of slow mount points.
- Slow mount points don't affect the rest (no gaps).
